author: LHSummers
text: What is the overall potential? We estimated it would be possible to close 15% of the tax gap by spending approximately $100B on additional enforcement, as would be necessary to return the #IRS to its historical scale. Every $1 spent would generate $11 in greater tax collection.

author: LHSummers
text: When third-party income reports exist to compare to individual tax returns, income is correctly reported more than 95 percent of the time. Almost all income earned by individuals who make $200,000 or less annually gets reported in this way.

author: LHSummers
text: The IRS invests less than a quarter as much in information technology as major banks and still relies on systems from the 1960s. Pilot projects suggest payoff rates on strategic IT investments could approach 50:1.

author: LHSummers
text: Fewer than 1 percent of corporate returns were audited in 2018 — even though corporate audits on average raised nearly $1 million in additional revenue.

author: LHSummers
text: Only 5 percent of taxpayers earning above $5 million are audited — even though IRS data demonstrates that an extra auditor-hour spent on their returns raises almost $5,000 on average.

author: LHSummers
text: At present, recipients of the earned-income tax credit — all of whom have incomes below $50,000 — are about as likely as those making $500,000 or more to be audited.

author: LHSummers
text: Enforcement effort — as reflected in the share of gross collections reinvested in the IRS — has declined by approximately 35 percent over the past decade, and the decline has been disproportionate for corporations and millionaires.

author: LHSummers
text: @washingtonpost @NatashaRSarin Extrapolating from the most recently available IRS information, the tax gap will be more than $7.5 trillion over a decade. You only need to close 15 percent of this gap to raise $1 trillion.

author: LHSummers
text: Our new analysis suggests that better-focused audits, raising IRS enforcement to previous peak levels, investing in information technology and broadening earnings reporting could raise more than $1 trillion in the next decade, primarily from very high-income taxpayers.

author: LHSummers
text: @paulkrugman I share the views of many including Krugman & Sen Warren that moneyed interest like Koch brothers have toxic impacts on policy and politics. My issue is that I believe wealth taxes are not useful and could even be counterproductive as a strategy for reasons laid out in my tweets.

author: LHSummers
text: Don't follow, @PaulKrugman. My point was that a wealth tax would reduce the after tax price faced for influence activities, and so could easily encourage them. It certainly would not reduce wealth enough to matter for politics.

quoted.text: Hate to say this, but Larry is just wrong on the political economy here. Two words: Koch brothers. Influence goes far beyond campaign contributions; climate denial, for example, is driven by a network of disinformation institutions 1/

author: LHSummers
text: I regret my use of Henry Ford as an example and my reference to anti-Semitism brought more heat than light. And, of course, I don’t think wealth taxes promote anti-Semitism. I was using Ford as an example of a wealthy person with noxious views.

author: LHSummers
text: Such giving would happen much earlier in life with a wealth tax and SZ suggest there might be more pressure to spend quickly. This, for good or ill, would raise the political influence of the rich.

author: LHSummers
text: Foundation wealth raises an interesting set of issues. Of course, as many point out, the Ford Foundation began as a response to estate taxation.

author: LHSummers
text: Apologies. One of my wealth tax tweets was misunderstood. The point I was trying to make was that a wealth tax could induce the wealthy to spend more of their money, incl. on political expression in line w their beliefs, vs. after their death when funds are directed by a board.

author: LHSummers
text: There are better ways to spur increases in middle class wages, to avoid the recession that is more likely than not in the next two years, and to meet the Chinese economic challenge than a narrow focus on wealth taxation.

author: LHSummers
text: Premising a progressive agenda on a financing source that is untried and likely to be declared unconstitutional is risking what could be a great window of opportunity.

author: LHSummers
text: Great progressive achievements like Social Security and Medicare happened because seeds were planted that grew over long time periods and were implemented thoughtfully.

author: LHSummers
text: Finally the politics of the wealth tax seem problematic at multiple levels. Successful progressive policies such as those in place in Northern Europe rely not on soaking the rich but on broadly levied taxes like the VAT that support a state that is generous to the middle class.

author: LHSummers
text: I think the case for a well-designed financial transactions tax like that in place in Hong Kong is stronger than the case for a wealth tax. It should be seriously considered.

author: LHSummers
text: Further steps would include raising the corporate rate to 27 percent and repealing various shelters legislated in the Trump tax bill. Full taxation of dividends, and estate tax reform would also raise needed revenue.

author: LHSummers
text: The agenda would start w beefed-up tax enforcement tilted towards high-income. Next would be capital gains reform to include constructive realization at death & on charitable gifts, raising rates, elimination of carried interest & tax-free like kind exchanges of real estate, etc

author: LHSummers
text: What about raising revenue?  Controlling avoidance and closing loopholes and shelters could raise more than Saez and @gabriel_zucman claim for a wealth tax and much more than it would in fact raise.

author: LHSummers
text: Government should also scale back its advocacy abroad of commercial interests largely unrelated to US jobs. And it should limit programs where businesses get privileged access to government officials by contributing to worthy causes.

author: LHSummers
text: Correct approach also involves leveling the playing field for union organizing and stepping up business regulation especially in the areas of antitrust and consumer protection.

author: LHSummers
text: One proposal: requiring high-ranking federal officials from the President on down to file financial disclosure forms for 3 years after they leave office.

author: LHSummers
text: The right progressive agenda around money and power involves political reform directed at changing campaign finance rules, limiting lobbying and revolving-door activities.

author: LHSummers
text: There may also be some areas—particularly involving corporations—where taxes based on market value could usefully replace or backstop income tax approaches.

author: LHSummers
text: I hope observers will look back on the wealth tax debate as an extremely clever way of broadening the tax reform Overton window. If so, it could be very valuable, as much needs to be done to address stagnant middle class wages and the excess political power of moneyed interests.

author: LHSummers
text: While the wealth tax currently polls fairly well, I am struck that in last half century, the economics of candidates Warren & Sanders most resembles George McGovern, who later regretted his anti-business tone and lost badly to Nixon, the past President who most resembles Trump.

author: LHSummers
text: Wealth taxes have the additional problem in the United States that they are likely to be found unconstitutional.

author: LHSummers
text: ...or that through closely-held corps, depletion allowances, other shelters, and egregious payments of non-taxable compensation this was an era of massive avoidance, which helps explain why the income distribution looks egalitarian.

author: LHSummers
text: SZ treat the era of 90 percent top income tax rates as a golden age. They do not acknowledge that serious researchers think this was beyond the revenue maximizing rate......

author: LHSummers
text: Nor do they acknowledge that you can get credit lines against homes; but not private businesses.

author: LHSummers
text: SZ cite the property tax on homeowners as an example of a successful wealth tax. They do not point out that the imputed rent on homes is not taxed, even though mortgage interest can be deducted, so the property tax fills a tax gap.

author: LHSummers
text: This point is reinforced by the observation that wealth taxes do not share risk as income taxes do, in part because there is no provision for loss offsets when assets go down in value.

author: LHSummers
text: Think of investors that pay less than a 2-percent interest rate, or those who lose money on their investments, or those who are already paying corporate taxes, dividend taxes and capital gains on their assets.

author: LHSummers
text: It is demagogic to say that a wealth tax has no incentive effects because it is only levied at a 2 or 3 percent rate. Judged as a tax on income it can easily lead to rates over 100 percent.

author: LHSummers
text: If, as is conservative, SZ overstate high-end wealth by 1/3, compliance by 1/3 (which assumes their wealth tax is far better collected than estate tax) & one corrects their errors in computing a 10-year projection, the right revenue estimate is less than half the one they provide

author: LHSummers
text: They also assume, implausibly, that nominal GDP will grow at 5.5 percent mis-citing the CBO.  In fact, the CBO has a much more modest 4 percent projection.

author: LHSummers
text: 3rd, it is absurd to assume, as SZ do, that the wealth tax can be immediately implemented.

author: LHSummers
text: 2nd, experience w the estate tax demonstrates that this kind of tax is very hard to enforce. Wealth can be spread among family members, it can be mis-valued where there are not liquid markets, and it can be given to charity. All of this would happen if a wealth tax was introduced

author: LHSummers
text: The SZ revenue estimates are overstatements by a factor of 2 or more. First, as work by Matt Smith, @omzidar, and Eric Zwick shows, SZ overstate the wealth of those with more than $50M by a wide margin.

author: LHSummers
text: Saez and @gabriel_zucman are also way off on how much revenue wealth taxation will deliver, a point we’ve made in the past. https://t.co/LxYByQhTMQ

author: LHSummers
text: At our @PIIE  discussion, Saez was unable to provide even a single example of a specific instance of excessive political power that the wealth tax would address.

author: LHSummers
text: Forcing the wealthy to spend could boomerang. If the wealth tax had been in place a century ago, we would have had more anti-semitism from Henry Ford and a smaller Ford Foundation today.

author: LHSummers
text: Very few of the problems today involve personal contributions of the wealthy. They instead involve corporate contributions or large groups: e.g., the NRA, the insurance industry, sugar producers…

author: LHSummers
text: It costs $5 million a year at maximum to be a central player in either party. This will be easily affordable for the rich even with a wealth tax.

author: LHSummers
text: The argument that a wealth tax will usefully address the excess role of the rich influencing politics is very weak. To be sure, there is a very real problem, but the wealth tax will not be remotely effective in addressing it.

author: LHSummers
text: A further issue is that when wealth goes up because of lower discount factors (eg a higher stock market PE ratio), sustainable income or spending does not change, so it's questionable whether wealth holders are better off. Those seeking to grow spending indefinitely are worse off

author: LHSummers
text: Wealth inequality is a highly problematic basis for judging a society. Consider a country that put in place super effective social insurance against retirement, disability & health expenses. Middle class people would run their “standby assets” down & wealth inequality would go up

author: LHSummers
text: SZ make much of a set of claims regarding the Forbes 400 and particularly the low taxes they paid in 2018. How can they know? The Forbes 400 in most cases only filed their taxes in the last week. All their claims about the Forbes 400 are made with no reference to actual tax data.

author: LHSummers
text: Since 1950 we have greatly expanded progressive social insurance largely funded by payroll levies. SZ treat this as the tax system becoming more regressive when obviously government policy has become more redistribtional if, as is proper, you include benefits.

author: LHSummers
text: First, I have carefully studied the Twitter conversations regarding Saez and Zucman’s (SZ) work. I find their critics largely convincing. Some specific issues:

author: LHSummers
text: The role of monied interests in shaping policy is also a crucial political problem. Wealth taxation is not an effective approach to any of these problems.

author: LHSummers
text: Lack of income growth and opportunity for middle class families is a fundamental problem in American society. So too is rising inequality.

author: LHSummers
text: Last week, I had the chance to debate Emmanuel Saez at the @PIIE. Here is a video of the discussion https://t.co/YJdjV4c4Th and a series of tweets explaining my disagreements with Saez and Zucman’s approach; and proposing alternatives to a singular focus on wealth taxation.

author: LHSummers
text: Right emphasis is to make sure taxes are more progressive than they are now but not an emphasis that the salvation for United States is tearing down the wealthy --- that was McGovern premise and it didn't work.

author: LHSummers
text: If we define our entire the economic debate around wages not growing enough, around a fight between workers & businesses, we are not going to do the kind of things that got us out of the depression and that won us WWII ---pulling together as a country.

author: LHSummers
text: Inequality is a crucial concern but so is the fact that the American economy is stagnating and may go into a recession next year. So too is the fact that our leadership as largest economy in the word is being threatened by China.

author: LHSummers
text: The campaign proposals that the wealth tax reminds me most of are George McGovern’s --- with the same kind of redistribution emphasis which didn't work for progressive cause as it led to Richard Nixon's re-election.

author: LHSummers
text: .....rather than focusing on cooperatively making investments we need to compete to have the stronger economy that is necessary for everybody's prosperity.

author: LHSummers
text: What I am against, at a time when we are fighting for our competitiveness and economic leadership in world with China, is an approach that at its center is pitting workers against companies and some Americans against other Americans....

author: LHSummers
text: I am for more progressive taxation to enable crucial public investments in everything from children, to health care, to greater competitiveness.

author: LHSummers
text: The need to absorb saving if reasonable levels of employment and output are to be maintained drives major increases in current and prospective fiscal deficits.  Lower rates of return raise the present value of long term liabilities like pensions.

author: LHSummers
text: Low rates also encourage asset price inflation. This in turn drives financialization as financial activity like investment advising moves w/ total value of assets.

author: LHSummers
text: It is the reason for very low nominal and real interest rates and consequent increases in public and private sector leverage and debt accumulation.

author: LHSummers
text: Most clearly, it is the reason for sluggish real growth and the inability of central banks to achieve their inflation targets.

author: LHSummers
text: By almost any measure, U.S. citizens no longer share a common lived experience. Men age 25 to 54 in Arlington, Va., have a 5 percent chance of being without work. Men in Flint, Mich., have more than 35 percent chance of that.

author: LHSummers
text: The economic geography of the USA is central to our most serious economic social and political problems. And yet it is a subject that receives only the episodic attention of federal policymakers and initiatives that are far too small to have a meaningful chance of success.

author: LHSummers
text: It’s hard to imagine our profession or my career without him. Thank you my mentor and my friend and may you Rest In Peace.

author: LHSummers
text: Teacher, scholar, public official, public intellectual, academic entrepreneur, mentor, close friend. It’s hard to imagine anything economists do where Marty did not excel.

author: LHSummers
text: Marty, as well as anyone I knew, wove together the roles of public intellectual and academic economist. Unlike many engaged with policy, he tested his ideas with academic stars but he also never forgot the importance of both learning from and reaching a broad audience.

author: LHSummers
text: In Washington, and for that matter every place else, I never saw him say a truly nasty thing or make an ad hominem argument.  His first loyalty was never to a party or a President but to the truth as he saw it.

author: LHSummers
text: Washington is often not a nice place. In the face of plenty of counter evidence, Marty maintained his faith in the power of ideas and good faith analytical advocacy.

author: LHSummers
text: Forty years later, the individual papers have often been superseded but the lessons that incentives matter, that taxes and spending and social insuring shape them, and that economists can measure them and make the world work better surely endure.

author: LHSummers
text: Then Marty started publishing a paper a month in a major journal demonstrating a previously undocumented incentive effect of a tax, spending or social insurance program.

author: LHSummers
text: Ideas that economists today take for granted, above all that public policies have major incentive effects and that people and businesses respond strongly to incentives had fallen out of the professional economic discourse by the late 1960s.

author: LHSummers
text: Better managed economies can, history teaches, be the difference between war and peace.

author: LHSummers
text: I learned from Marty that summer that economics was not a field but a calling. A doctor could treat and help a patient.  An economist could raise the standard of living of millions who would never know his or her name.

author: LHSummers
text: My project involved extending Marty’s work on social security and saving by looking at international comparisons.

author: LHSummers
text: It is hard for me to think about carrying on my career as an economist without Marty Feldstein. I first met Marty in 1973, when he hired me as part of his flotilla of a dozen or so research assistants.

text: @WSJ In the black hole, weak economic growth and low inflation lead to low interest rates, and falling confidence makes it hard to escape low rates.

author: LHSummers
text: @WSJ Japan is unable to escape, and it doesn’t look like Europe will. The US did escape, but it looks like we’re being pulled back in. We’re only one recession away from “Japanification.”

author: LHSummers
text:
@WSJ WSJ: Tell us about your black-hole theory.
MR. SUMMERS: The experience in Japan, Europe, or even the U.S., is that once you get into a near-zero interest-rate regime, it’s kind of a black hole. The economy tends to be pulled in, and once there, it’s difficult to escape.

author: LHSummers
text:
@WSJ WSJ: Does the consumer sector provide a bulwark against recession?
MR. SUMMERS: I don’t think so. Consumer psychology is a volatile thing. If consumers sense things are turning the wrong way, it could change quite rapidly.

author: LHSummers
text:
@WSJ WSJ: Why is strong employment a risk?
MR. SUMMERS: It has limited room to get better, given how strong it is. And we don’t have a successful history with contained increases in unemployment once they start.
